{background-color="#1B3A6B"} # Brief recap 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Module 06: getting data from the web ### What we did in lectures 18 and 19 :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - A web API is a [contract]{.alert} between your code and a server - We built URLs, read status codes, and followed paths through [JSON]{.alert} - `curl` and `requests` fetched the data - A `for` loop turned the reply into a DataFrame - We saved a [snapshot]{.alert}, so the analysis gives the same numbers every time - Today: what happens when the data get [really big?]{.alert} ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - This module is about [scaling]{.alert}: making code cope with more data - Sometimes the answer is [parallel code]{.alert}: several cores working at once - Sometimes it is a [better algorithm]{.alert} - Sometimes it is a [faster engine]{.alert}, like DuckDB (next lecture) :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 20px;"} Lecture 19's course panel, `wdi_panel.parquet`, uses the parquet format we meet later today ::: ::: ::: ::: # Today's agenda {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Lecture outline ### What we will cover today :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Serial and parallel]{.alert} code, and the `map` function - [`joblib`]{.alert} and [`concurrent.futures`]{.alert}: parallel work on your laptop - [Big O notation]{.alert}: what parallelism can and cannot fix - [Amdahl's law]{.alert}: the limit on speed-up - [The GIL]{.alert}: why threads do not always help in Python - [Dask]{.alert} for data bigger than your memory - Lazy arrays and DataFrames - CSV and parquet files - `dask.delayed` for your own functions - [Best practices]{.alert}: when to parallelise, and when not to ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -30px;"} [![](figures/cores.webp){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cores.webp"} [![](figures/dask.png){width="55%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dask.png"} ::: ::: ::: ::: # Serial vs parallel algorithms {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Serial execution and the `map` function ### One line finishes before the next one starts :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Python normally runs one line after another, in order - This loop calls `bar` on each number, one at a time: :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#f9d72220 .cell cache='true' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np # An array of six numbers foo = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) # A function that squares a number def bar(x): return x * x # Call bar on each element, in order for element in foo: print(bar(element)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 1 4 9 16 25 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [`map`]{.alert} applies one function to every element of a list - Here is my own version, so you can see the loop inside: :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#fbca9ec4 .cell cache='true' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def my_map(function, array): output = [] # empty list for the results for element in array: output.append(function(element)) return output my_map(bar, foo) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(4), np.int64(9), np.int64(16), np.int64(25)] ``` ::: ::: ::: - Python has a [built-in `map`](https://www.w3schools.com/python/ref_func_map.asp): :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#543f7279 .cell cache='true' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} list(map(bar, foo)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(4), np.int64(9), np.int64(16), np.int64(25)] ``` ::: ::: ::: - Same answer, one line. Use the built-in one ::: ::: ::: ## Using `joblib` for parallel computing ### Two functions turn a loop into parallel work :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Each call to `bar` is [independent]{.alert}, so the calls can run at the same time - Your CPU has several [cores]{.alert}. Each core runs one task at a time - [`joblib`](https://joblib.readthedocs.io/) sends tasks to [worker processes]{.alert}: separate copies of Python, one per core - `Parallel(n_jobs=6)` runs up to six tasks at once. `n_jobs=-1` uses all cores - `delayed(bar)` wraps `bar`, so joblib runs it later, on a worker - `delayed(bar)(x) for x in foo` makes one task per element - That is a [generator expression]{.alert}: a `for` loop inside brackets ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Using our `bar` function and `foo` array from before: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#ca971090 .cell cache='true' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Install joblib if you haven't done so yet # !pip install joblib from joblib import Parallel, delayed results = Parallel(n_jobs=6)( delayed(bar)(x) for x in foo ) results ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [np.int64(0), np.int64(1), np.int64(4), np.int64(9), np.int64(16), np.int64(25)] ``` ::: ::: ::: - Each worker gets a different element of `foo` - The results match the serial version, because the work is the same ::: ::: ::: ## Serial vs parallel execution ### Four heavy calls, timed for real :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `calculation` runs ten heavy steps on ten million random numbers - The calls do not depend on each other. The problem is [embarrassingly parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embarrassingly_parallel) - [`%timeit`](https://ipython.readthedocs.io/en/stable/interactive/magics.html#magic-timeit){.alert} runs a line several times and reports the average time. It works in Jupyter only - `%%timeit` (two `%` signs) times a whole cell - [One call:]{.alert} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#7988ac99 .cell cache='true' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} def calculation(size=10000000): # Create a large array and perform operations arr = np.random.rand(size) for _ in range(10): arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr) return np.mean(arr) # Single run %timeit calculation() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 326 ms ± 2.75 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [Four calls, one after another:]{.alert} - `_` is the usual name for a loop variable we do not use :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#0ecdee2e .cell cache='true' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Sequential runs (4 times) %timeit [calculation() for _ in range(4)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1.31 s ± 8.34 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - [Four calls, in parallel:]{.alert} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#8c75c219 .cell cache='true' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} %%timeit # Parallel runs (4 times) Parallel(n_jobs=4)( delayed(calculation)() for _ in range(4) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 464 ms ± 4.55 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - It is not a full 4× speed-up, because [starting workers and collecting results takes time]{.alert}. The saving is still real ::: ::: ::: # concurrent.futures {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## `concurrent.futures`: the standard-library option ### The same pattern ships with Python itself :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [`concurrent.futures`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html) comes with Python: nothing to install - Slow code is either [computing]{.alert} or [waiting]{.alert} - Computing ([CPU-bound]{.alert}): use processes, with [`ProcessPoolExecutor`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor) - Waiting ([I/O-bound]{.alert}): use threads, with [`ThreadPoolExecutor`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor) - A [thread]{.alert} is a light worker that shares its process's memory - `with` starts the workers and stops them at the end :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#ae5df22f .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as executor: results = list(executor.map(bar, foo)) ``` ::: ::: - In a notebook on macOS or Windows, [import `bar` from a `.py` file]{.alert}. Workers cannot see functions defined in a cell. joblib avoids this ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Threads start fast, and waiting needs no extra core - Each URL asks the [World Bank API](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/898581-api-basic-call-structures) for one country's population :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#2c65d02b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor import requests base = "https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/" end = "/indicator/SP.POP.TOTL?format=json&per_page=100" urls = [base + "BRA" + end, base + "IND" + end, base + "USA" + end] def fetch(url): return requests.get(url, timeout=30).json() with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor: results = list(executor.map(fetch, urls)) ``` ::: ::: - Lecture 19 sent one request at a time. Here, all three wait at once ::: ::: ::: ## When to use which? ### joblib inside scikit-learn, and a summary :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [joblib]{.alert} suits numeric loops and [scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/) - scikit-learn uses joblib when you set `n_jobs=-1` - [`load_digits()`](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.datasets.load_digits.html) loads 1,797 small images of handwritten digits :::{style="font-size: 1.1em;"} ::: {#ca34b0cf .cell cache='true' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.datasets import load_digits from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV from sklearn.svm import SVC import time digits = load_digits() param_grid = {"C": [0.1, 1, 10], "gamma": [0.001, 0.01]} start = time.time() search = GridSearchCV(SVC(), param_grid, cv=3, n_jobs=-1) search.fit(digits.data, digits.target) elapsed = time.time() - start print(f"Best score: {search.best_score_:.3f}") print(f"Time: {elapsed:.2f}s (all cores)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Best score: 0.976 Time: 1.93s (all cores) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [`concurrent.futures`]{.alert} suits downloads, and machines where you cannot install packages :::{style="margin-top: 30px; margin-bottom: 30px;"} | Scenario | Tool | |----------|------| | sklearn / numeric loops | `joblib` (`n_jobs=-1`) | | Download many files | `ThreadPoolExecutor` | | CPU-heavy, no dependencies | `ProcessPoolExecutor` | | Bigger than RAM, clusters | `Dask` (next section) | ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 20px;"} [Every tool follows the same steps]{.alert}: split the work, run it on separate workers, then collect the results ::: ::: ::: ::: # Big O notation {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Big O notation ### Runtime growth decides whether parallelism helps :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Big O notation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation) describes how the runtime grows as the input grows - [O(1)]{.alert} means constant: reading one array element costs the same whatever the array size - [O(n)]{.alert} means linear: a single loop takes twice as long when the input doubles - [O(n²)]{.alert} means quadratic: a nested loop takes four times as long when the input doubles - Calling `calculation` on `n` inputs is [O(n)]{.alert}: a hundred calls take a hundred times as long as one ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center;"} ::: {#8526fdfc .cell cache='true' execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np # Simulate processing times num_images = np.array([1, 10, 50, 100, 200]) sequential_time = num_images * 2 # 2 seconds per image parallel_time = (num_images * 2) / 4 # 4 cores, ideal speedup plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) plt.plot(num_images, sequential_time, 'o-', label='Serial O(n)', linewidth=2, markersize=8) plt.plot(num_images, parallel_time, 's-', label='Parallel on 4 cores (still O(n))', linewidth=2, markersize=8) plt.xlabel('Number of Images', fontsize=12) plt.ylabel('Time (seconds)', fontsize=12) plt.title('O(n) Scaling: Serial vs Parallel', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold') plt.legend(fontsize=11) plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](21-parallel-computing_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=670 height=454} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## What parallelism does to complexity ### Cores divide the time, but the growth rate stays the same :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - With `p` cores, an O(n) task takes about [n/p time plus overhead]{.alert}. It is still O(n) - Four cores make it almost 4× faster, minus the cost of running the workers - The best candidates are [embarrassingly parallel O(n) tasks]{.alert}, such as one function applied to `n` separate inputs - These tasks share no data and do not wait for each other :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 20px;"} Parallelism never changes the Big O class. It only divides the time by a constant, so O(n²) on eight cores is still O(n²) ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [A poor candidate for parallelism:]{.alert} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#7731d319 .cell cache='true' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # O(n^2): every pair of elements def pairwise_sum(data): n = len(data) results = [] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): results.append(data[i] + data[j]) return results data = list(range(1_000)) print(f"{len(pairwise_sum(data)):,} operations") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1,000,000 operations ``` ::: ::: ::: - 1,000 elements give 1 million operations - `n = 100_000` gives 10 billion. Eight cores still leave 1.25 billion each - Other poor candidates: - Steps that need results from a previous step - Tasks that share the same data - Tasks limited by memory, not by the CPU ::: ::: ::: ## Try it yourself! 🧠 {#sec:exercise01} :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} 1. Install the packages with `pip install joblib numpy` if you have not done so already 2. Run the serial version below and write down the time it prints. `np.arange(1000000)` makes an array of the numbers 0 to 999,999 :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#5753f765 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np def square(x): return x**2 # Create a large array to process numbers = np.arange(1000000) # Sequential version %timeit [square(x) for x in numbers] ``` ::: ::: 3. Now run the parallel version and write down its time as well. Be patient, as this one takes a while :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#52536320 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} from joblib import Parallel, delayed # Parallel version %timeit Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(square)(x) for x in numbers) ``` ::: ::: 4. Compare the two times and decide which version you would use [[Appendix 01]{.button}](#sec:appendix01) ::: # Amdahl's law {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Amdahl's law: the speed-up ceiling ### The serial share caps the speed-up :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Some parts of a program [cannot run in parallel]{.alert}: setup, merging results, or steps that wait for the one before - That part is the [serial share]{.alert} $s$. The rest, $p = 1 - s$, can be split across cores - More cores only speed up $p$, so $s$ sets a ceiling ([Amdahl's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law)) - $\text{speedup} = \dfrac{1}{s + \dfrac{p}{N}}$, with $N$ = number of cores - Example: 90% parallel ($s = 0.1$) on 8 cores gives $\frac{1}{0.1 + 0.9/8} = \frac{1}{0.2125} \approx 4.7\times$, not $8\times$ - Even with infinite cores, the serial 10% remains, so the limit is $1/0.1 = 10\times$ ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center;"} ::: {#3baacbaf .cell cache='true' execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np cores = np.arange(1, 65) serial_fracs = [0.05, 0.2, 0.5] labels = ["5% serial", "20% serial", "50% serial"] colours = ["#1B3A6B", "#E07A24", "#2CA02C"] plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5)) for s, lab, c in zip(serial_fracs, labels, colours): speedup = 1 / (s + (1 - s) / cores) plt.plot(cores, speedup, label=lab, linewidth=2, color=c) plt.xlabel("Number of cores", fontsize=12) plt.ylabel("Speed-up (×)", fontsize=12) plt.title("Amdahl's law: speed-up vs core count", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold") plt.legend(fontsize=11) plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](21-parallel-computing_files/figure-revealjs/cell-16-output-1.png){width=759 height=469} ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## The GIL ### Why threads do not always help in Python :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - CPython, the usual Python, has a [Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Interpreter_Lock) - Only [one thread]{.alert} runs Python code at a time - Threads help code that [waits]{.alert}: the lock is released during downloads - Threads do not help code that [computes]{.alert} - For computing, use [processes]{.alert}, each with its own GIL - [NumPy](https://numpy.org/) [releases the GIL]{.alert} in its C code, so threads can help there - [Polars](https://polars.dev/) and [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) use all cores on their own - Python 3.14 offers a [free-threaded build]{.alert} without the GIL ([PEP 779](https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/)), but not by default ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Which tool for which task: :::{style="font-size: 20px;"} | Task | Use | Why | |------|-----|-----| | Number crunching | [Processes]{.alert} (`joblib`, `ProcessPoolExecutor`) | Each has its own GIL | | Downloading many URLs | [Threads]{.alert} (`ThreadPoolExecutor`) | GIL released while waiting | | NumPy | [Threads can help]{.alert} | GIL released in C code | | Polars / DuckDB | [Neither]{.alert} | Already use all cores | | `sklearn` with `n_jobs=-1` | Processes (via `joblib`) | Each fold trains independently | ::: ::: ::: ::: # Dask {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Dask ### Familiar pandas code on data bigger than your RAM :::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} - [Dask](https://dask.org/) is a Python library for parallel computing - It handles [data bigger than your RAM](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/best-practices.html){.alert}, and runs on [clusters](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/deploying.html) of many machines - You write [NumPy](https://numpy.org/) or [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/) code, and Dask runs it in parallel - Its [task scheduler](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/scheduling.html){.alert} splits the work into small tasks and spreads them over your cores - It offers [arrays](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/array.html){.alert}, [DataFrames](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/dataframe.html){.alert} and [bags](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/bag.html){.alert} (parallel lists) - It is actively developed ([2026.8.0](https://github.com/dask/dask/releases/tag/2026.8.0), August 2026) - Next lecture times the same group-by in DuckDB, pandas and Dask ::: :::{.column width="48%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/dask-homepage-2026.png){width="88%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dask-homepage-2026.png"} :::{style="font-size: 17px;"} ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px; text-align: left;"} `joblib` splits the work into function calls. [Dask also splits the data into chunks]{.alert}, so the data can be bigger than your RAM ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Dask arrays ### NumPy arrays split into chunks, and nothing runs until `.compute()` :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#e5337d61 .cell cache='true' execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} import dask.dataframe as dd import dask.array as da ``` ::: ::: - A [Dask array](https://docs.dask.org/en/stable/array.html) splits a large array into [chunks]{.alert} - Each chunk is a [NumPy array](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.ndarray.html), processed in parallel - Here each chunk is 100 by 100: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#31cff20b .cell cache='true' execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} data = np.random.normal(size=100000).reshape(200, 500) a = da.from_array(data, chunks=(100, 100)) a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}
Array Chunk
Bytes 781.25 kiB 78.12 kiB
Shape (200, 500) (100, 100)
Dask graph 10 chunks in 1 graph layer
Data type float64 numpy.ndarray
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Dask arrays are [lazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazy_evaluation): Dask plans the steps but does not run them yet - Planning first helps Dask [save memory]{.alert} - Slicing gives a plan, not numbers: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#882d0770 .cell cache='true' execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} a[:10, 5] # first 10 rows of the 6th column ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
Array Chunk
Bytes 80 B 80 B
Shape (10,) (10,)
Dask graph 1 chunks in 2 graph layers
Data type float64 numpy.ndarray
``` ::: ::: ::: - `.compute()` runs the plan: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#cae4104b .cell cache='true' execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} a[:10, 5].compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` array([-1.03937332, -0.11820134, 0.25084186, -0.13490562, 1.5938117 , -0.74026513, 1.76553919, -0.15280199, -0.251494 , 1.4476932 ]) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Dask arrays ### Most NumPy operations work, and big ones can run faster :::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 21px;"} - Maths (`+`, `*`, `exp`, `log`) and summaries (`sum()`, `mean()`, `std()`) work as in NumPy :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#c9b9b1cd .cell cache='true' execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} a.sum().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` np.float64(-466.7794356795441) ``` ::: ::: ::: - The same operation on 100 million numbers, first in NumPy: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#08a6e78f .cell cache='true' execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} size = 100000000 np_arr = np.random.random(size) %timeit np_result = np.sqrt(np_arr) + np.sin(np_arr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 406 ms ± 8.81 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - Then in Dask, with automatic chunks: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#f9268327 .cell cache='true' execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} da_arr = da.random.random(size, chunks='auto') %timeit (da.sqrt(da_arr) + da.sin(da_arr)).compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 303 ms ± 14.7 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} [Not a rule]{.alert}: here NumPy uses one core and Dask uses several. Write down the three timings before you look at the appendix ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 22px; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px;"} ```python import numpy as np import dask.array as da size = 10_000_000 # Dask with SMALL chunks da_data_small = da.random.random(size, chunks=100_000) # 100 chunks %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_small**2).mean().compute() # Dask with MEDIUM chunks da_data_medium = da.random.random(size, chunks=2_000_000) # 5 chunks %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_medium**2).mean().compute() # Dask with LARGE chunks da_data_large = da.random.random(size, chunks=5_000_000) # 2 chunks %timeit da.sqrt(da_data_large**2).mean().compute() ``` ::: - [[Appendix 02]{.button}](#sec:appendix02) ::: ::: ::: # Read and write data with Dask {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Reading and writing data ### Thirty daily CSV files from one line of Dask :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - CSV is still the most common data format - pandas loads the [whole file into memory]{.alert} first - A big file can fill your RAM, even if you need one column - Dask reads and writes CSV in [partitions]{.alert}: [pieces of the table](https://docs.dask.org/en/latest/dataframe-create.html) - Here, one partition per day. Dask replaces the `*` in `'data/*.csv'` with each name - `name(i)` turns partition `i` into a date - Result: 30 files, 1 to 30 January 2000 - The `;` hides the file list that `to_csv` returns ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 22px; margin-top: 20px; margin-bottom: 20px;"} ::: {#8f06035b .cell cache='true' execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} df = dask.datasets.timeseries() df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: - The same group-by, on parquet: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#1ac9cdee .cell cache='true' execution_count=39} ``` {.python .cell-code} %timeit df.groupby('name').x.mean().compute() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 66.8 ms ± 537 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Why Parquet? ### Column storage reads only what you ask for :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - CSV is [row-based]{.alert}, so reading one column still means scanning every row - Parquet is [column-based]{.alert}, so it reads the columns you name and skips the others | Feature | CSV | Parquet | |---------|-----|---------| | Storage | Row-based | Column-based | | Compression | None | Snappy/gzip | | Column selection | Reads all | Reads only needed | | Data types | Text only | Typed (int, float, date) | | Our January 2000 data | 182 MB | 86 MB | ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - pandas reads both formats too: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#a38eaef5 .cell cache='true' execution_count=40} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd # CSV: reads every column, guesses the types one_day = pd.read_csv("data/2000-01-01.csv") print(one_day.shape) # Parquet: reads only the columns you name month = pd.read_parquet("data/2000-01.parquet", columns=["name", "x"]) print(month.shape) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (86400, 5) (2592000, 2) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} [CSV is not obsolete]{.alert}. Use parquet for files over 100 MB, or with [many columns]{.alert} when you need only a few. Keep CSV for small files and anything a colleague will open in Excel ::: ::: ::: ::: # Dask delayed {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Dask delayed ### A decorator schedules any function you already have :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - `dask.delayed` parallelises functions you already have - No Dask DataFrame or array needed - First, four calls in a row: :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#3a9cbe4b .cell cache='true' execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code} def calculation(size=10000000): arr = np.random.rand(size) for _ in range(10): arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr) return np.mean(arr) %timeit [calculation() for _ in range(4)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1.39 s ± 21.1 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - A [decorator]{.alert} is an `@` line above a `def`. It changes what the function does - With `@dask.delayed`, calling the function creates a task instead of running it :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#a583d755 .cell cache='true' execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code} @dask.delayed def delayed_calculation(size=10000000): arr = np.random.rand(size) for _ in range(10): arr = np.sqrt(arr) + np.sin(arr) return np.mean(arr) results = [] for _ in range(4): results.append(delayed_calculation()) # Compute all results at once %timeit final_results = dask.compute(*results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 515 ms ± 12.1 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: ::: - `dask.compute(*results)` runs all four tasks. The `*` passes the list items one by one ::: ::: ::: ## Dask delayed ### Dask draws the plan before running a single task :::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} - Three functions on three input sizes: nine tasks in three branches :::{style="font-size: 1.2em;"} ::: {#689abd25 .cell cache='true' execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code} @dask.delayed def generate_data(size): return np.random.rand(size) @dask.delayed def transform_data(data): return np.sqrt(data) + np.sin(data) @dask.delayed def aggregate_data(data): return { 'mean': np.mean(data), 'std': np.std(data), 'max': np.max(data) } sizes = [1000000, 2000000, 3000000] # Build the tasks (nothing runs yet) dask_results = [] for size in sizes: data = generate_data(size) transformed = transform_data(data) stats = aggregate_data(transformed) dask_results.append(stats) %timeit dask.compute(*dask_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 26.8 ms ± 495 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} - `dask.visualize()` draws the plan without running it :::{.taskgraph style="font-size: 1.2em; text-align: center;"} ::: {#dd07e647 .cell cache='true' execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Needs graphviz twice over: the Python package # and the binary itself # pip install graphviz # brew install graphviz (macOS) # apt install graphviz (Linux) dask.visualize(*dask_results) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=39} ![](21-parallel-computing_files/figure-revealjs/cell-44-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 10px;"} Dask sees all nine tasks first. The branches are independent, so they can run on separate workers ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The Dask dashboard ### Watching the task stream at `localhost:8787` :::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} - `from dask.distributed import Client`, then `client = Client()`, opens a dashboard at `localhost:8787` - Install it first: `pip install "dask[distributed]" bokeh` - The picture shows our three-step pipeline, run in a loop - Each row is one worker, and each coloured bar is one task - Purple is `generate_data`, teal is `transform_data`, and green is `aggregate_data` - Bars stacked on top of each other ran at the same time - It is the quickest way to check that your work really runs in parallel ::: :::{.column width="48%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/dask-dashboard-task-stream-2026.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/dask-dashboard-task-stream-2026.png"} :::{style="font-size: 17px;"} Dashboard at `localhost:8787`, running on my laptop ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} White space means an idle worker. Big gaps usually mean the chunks are too big, so there are fewer tasks than workers ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Best practices {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Best practices ### Cheaper fixes to try before you parallelise :::{style="margin-top: 20px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Measure first]{.alert}: `%timeit` and `cProfile` find the slow part. Amdahl's law says what fixing it is worth - [Check the tasks]{.alert}: are they independent, and big enough to be worth a worker? - [Better algorithm]{.alert}: $O(n \log n)$ beats parallel $O(n^2)$ on large inputs - [Better engine]{.alert}: DuckDB may beat parallel pandas (next lecture) - [Built-ins first]{.alert}: NumPy or pandas may already have a fast function - [Sample first]{.alert}: do you need all the data? ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [Use parquet]{.alert}: our parquet group-by was about 10× faster than CSV - [Call `.compute()` and `.persist()` rarely]{.alert}: each call runs the whole plan - [Try a few chunk sizes]{.alert}, or start with `chunks='auto'` - More tips in the [Dask best practices](https://docs.dask.org/en/latest/best-practices.html) :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 15px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 20px; margin-top: 15px;"} [Most common mistake]{.alert}: parallelising before measuring. More cores will not fix a slow disk or an $O(n^2)$ loop ::: ::: ::: ::: # Summary {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## What we learned today :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Serial and parallel code]{.alert}: `map`, embarrassingly parallel problems, `joblib` - [`concurrent.futures`]{.alert}: processes for CPU work, threads for waiting - [Big O notation]{.alert}: parallelism divides the time, but the growth rate stays the same - [Amdahl's law]{.alert}: the serial share caps the speed-up - [The GIL]{.alert}: threads for waiting, processes for computing ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - [Dask]{.alert}: lazy arrays and DataFrames for data bigger than RAM - [`dask.delayed`]{.alert} parallelises your own functions, and `dask.visualize` shows the plan - [Parquet]{.alert}: our January 2000 data went from 182 MB to 86 MB, with a much faster group-by - Next lecture, [SQL Revision with DuckDB]{.alert}: SQL on the WDI panel, and the same group-by in DuckDB, pandas and Dask :::{style="font-size: 18px;"} | Engine | Language | Parallel? | Out-of-core? | |--------|----------|-----------|-------------| | pandas | Python/C | Single-threaded | No | | Polars | Rust | All cores | Yes (streaming) | | DuckDB | C++ | All cores | Yes | | Dask | Python | All cores + clusters | Yes | ::: - Polars is covered in [tutorial 07](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/07-polars-tutorial.html) - SQL on DataFrames before then: [`tutorials/04-duckdb-sql-tutorial.qmd`](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/04-duckdb-sql-tutorial.html) ::: ::: ::: # Thank you! 😊 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Appendix 01 {#sec:appendix01} ### Solution to the joblib exercise :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#502dfa9e .cell cache='true' execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code} def square(x): return x**2 # Create a large array to process numbers = np.arange(1000000) # Sequential version %timeit [square(x) for x in numbers] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 46.8 ms ± 2.44 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10 loops each) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4700a8f0 .cell cache='true' execution_count=46} ``` {.python .cell-code} from joblib import Parallel, delayed # Parallel version %timeit Parallel(n_jobs=4)(delayed(square)(x) for x in numbers) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1.9 s ± 16.8 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each) ``` ::: ::: - [Expected result]{.alert}: the parallel version is [slower]{.alert} here - `square(x)` finishes so fast that the cost of sending a million tiny tasks to the workers swamps the work - Parallel computing pays off when each task is heavy [[Back to exercise]{.button}](#sec:exercise01) ::: ## Appendix 02 {#sec:appendix02} ### Chunk sizes compared :::{style="margin-top: 30px;
